summary:
North Korea's Criminal Code of 1950, revised in 2009, appears to contain no penalty for consensual same-sex acts. The same code supplies the provisions through which authorities act without reference to sexual orientation: Article 193 bans the import, keeping and distribution of "decadent culture," including sexual recordings, and Article 262 bans collective "obscene activities." Neither is defined in terms that constrain how the authorities apply it. Legislation enacted after the 2014 UN Commission of Inquiry report, including the Pyongyang Cultural Protection Act, tightened this control over expression and conduct.

The US State Department's 2022 human rights report on North Korea reaches the same position on the statute book: no specific law criminalises same-sex conduct, but the regime's total control leaves no space for LGBT life. Its 2020 report states that reliable information on LGBT persons is unavailable and that the repression of all civil society is the dominant human-rights reality in the country. The same department reports that no provisions in North Korean law prohibit discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and that the concepts do not appear in the law.

Gender identity has no standing in public life, though a narrow administrative route exists. A sex-marker change on a birth certificate or citizen card is reported to be technically possible under "unavoidable circumstances": an application to the People's Security Agency plus a state forensic medical evaluation, with surgical intervention required in practice. No law explicitly bans gender-affirming care, but the under-resourced health system makes hormones and surgery effectively inaccessible. The Constitution, last revised in 2024, does not address discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity.

The regime's official posture combines denial with hostility. A KCNA commentary of 22 April 2014 rejected the UN Commission of Inquiry's report as a political fabrication and personally attacked commissioner Michael Kirby as "a disgusting old lecher with a 40-odd-year-long career of homosexuality," an attempt to discredit the findings by reference to homosexuality itself. A 2014 KCNA statement denied the existence of homosexuality in the country. There is no registration route for LGBTI organisations.

Accounts of violence conflict. Outright International records no documented state or non-state violence against LGBTIQ people in North Korea. Against that, a 2023 South Korean Ministry of Unification report of 584 pages cites defector testimony alleging that at least one male detainee in a detention camp was secretly executed for homosexuality in 2014, and a 2011 Korea Times report sourced to Free North Korea Radio claimed the execution of a lesbian couple, a North Korean woman and a Japanese woman, for being influenced by capitalism and bringing corruption of public morals. A 2017 defector account published by CNN records homosexuality's place in North Korean society and the punishment it carries.

Family law is explicit. Article 8 of the Family Law of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea states that marriage may be done only between one man and one woman, and as of 2026 no North Korean law recognises same-sex marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships. Same-sex couples could not legally adopt children, per the State Department's 2020 report.

Visibility carries personal cost. Jang Young-jin, a novelist who defected in the late 1990s, is documented as the first publicly known gay defector and was forcibly outed; he was profiled by BBC Korean in October 2024. An openly gay defector published an autobiography in 2017. Reporting on the country describes a collective-over-individual political order that forces sexual minorities into silent self-suppression.
tangentialFactors:
The absence of a defined homosexuality offence does not indicate tolerance; it reflects a legal order in which conduct is punished through broadly drafted provisions on culture, obscenity and public morals that officials apply at discretion. The 2014 UN Commission of Inquiry and the regime's rejection of it are the frame within which the country's LGBT record is assessed, and the state news agency's response treated the commissioner's sexuality as grounds for dismissal.

The 2020 State Department finding that reliable information is unavailable means the country's actual practice cannot be established from open sources, and the conflicting violence reports above should be read against that limitation. Repression of all civil society removes the organised constituency that would otherwise document incidents, so the absence of reported cases carries little evidentiary weight.

Comparison with neighbouring jurisdictions is of limited use here: several nearby legal orders moved to decriminalise or recognise same-sex relationships over the same period, while North Korea's framework remained without any such provision and without anti-discrimination protection.

outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether Articles 193 and 262 have ever been applied specifically against a person for homosexuality or gender expression is not sourced in the inventory. The 2014 camp execution allegation and the 2011 report of an executed lesbian couple rest on defector testimony and media sourcing and have not been independently corroborated; no outcome of any investigation is available.

Unresolved: whether any person has completed the documented sex-marker change procedure is not sourced, and no data in the inventory addresses entry screening, visa assessment, border questioning or document inspection for visitors, so the risk a trans traveller faces on arrival in North Korea cannot be stated from these sources.

Not sourced: whether Article 8 of the Family Law has been applied in any reported case, and whether the 2024 constitutional revision debate touched sexual orientation or gender identity beyond the reported silence on those terms.
